title: His last days
hook: Too weak to lead the prayer, he sent for Abu Bakr. His last words were about prayer and the people in your care.

screens.text: **Too weak to lead the prayer, he sent for Abu Bakr.** These are the last days of his life, so take this one gently. His final words were about prayer, and about the people in your care.

**He fell ill.** Early in 11 AH, back in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ fell ill, IslamQA reports [IslamQA 11575]. When prayer time came, he was too weak to lead it. Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people, he said [Bukhari 664].
bubbles: Told that Abu Bakr was too soft-hearted for it, he said it again, and again, until Abu Bakr led [Bukhari 664].

screens.prompt: You're in the masjid. Abu Bakr is leading. Then the Prophet ﷺ comes out, held up by two men, his feet dragging. Abu Bakr starts to step back. What happens?

options.text: He signals Abu Bakr to stay, and sits down beside him
options.feedback: That's what happened. Ill as he was, he came to pray with them and kept Abu Bakr in place [Bukhari 664].

options.text: He sends Abu Bakr away and stands to lead
options.feedback: Not quite. He signalled Abu Bakr to stay where he was, and was seated beside him [Bukhari 664].
Not quite. He came out to pray, too weak to stand, and sat beside Abu Bakr [Bukhari 664].

screens.text: **A daughter's tears.** His daughter Fatimah came to see him. Welcome, my daughter, he said, and sat her beside him. He whispered something, and she wept. He whispered again, and she laughed [Bukhari 3624].
bubbles: Aisha was watching. She said she had never seen happiness so close to sadness [Bukhari 3624].

screens.text: A few months after the Farewell Hajj.

events.title: Abu Bakr leads
events.text: Too weak to lead, he sends Abu Bakr [Bukhari 664].

events.title: The day he died
events.text: And the words that steadied everyone.

cards.back: He told her he would die soon. Every year Jibril had gone over the Qur'an with him once; that year, twice [Bukhari 3624].
He told her she would be the first of his family to follow him, and the leader of the believing women [Bukhari 3624].
She kept his secret while he lived. Only after he died did she tell Aisha [Bukhari 3624].

screens.text: **His last words.** Among the very last things he said: the prayer, the prayer, and fear Allah regarding those in your care [Abu Dawud 5156].
bubbles: At the end of everything, he was still thinking about salah, and about the people who depend on others.

screens.text: **What mattered most.** You've been building your prayers since Day 8. At the end of his life, prayer was still the first thing on his mind. Then the people in your care: a parent, a child, someone who depends on you. That's where he pointed.

screens.situation: Aaliyah's mom, who isn't Muslim, is in hospital, and Aaliyah spends every evening with her. She's been missing prayers and feels torn between her mom and her faith.

options.text: Keep caring for her mom, and pray quietly in a corner of the room or a hospital prayer room when it's time
options.feedback: Yes. Prayer and care for the people you love belong together. His last words held both.

options.text: Put prayer on hold until her mom gets better
options.feedback: Not quite. Prayer was the first thing on his mind even when he was dying. It goes with her.

options.text: Visit her mom less so she can keep her prayer schedule
options.feedback: Not quite. Caring for her mom is part of her faith too. She can do both.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- He fell ill early in 11 AH (IslamQA: in Safar) [IslamQA 11575] (single organisation; "IslamQA reports").
- In his final illness, when the adhan was called, he said to tell Abu Bakr to lead the people; told Abu Bakr was soft-hearted, he repeated it a third time. Feeling a little better, he came out supported by two men, his feet dragging; Abu Bakr began to step back; he signalled him to stay and was seated beside him [Bukhari 664].
- Fatimah came; he welcomed her as "my daughter", whispered and she wept, whispered again and she laughed; Aisha said she had never seen happiness so close to sadness. After his death Fatimah explained: Jibril had reviewed the Qur'an with him twice that year instead of once, which he took as a sign of his death; then that she would be the first of his family to follow him and the chief of the believing women [Bukhari 3624].
- In his last illness he said he still felt the pain of the food he ate at Khaybar [Bukhari 4428] (seerah-31).
- 'Ali reported his last words: the prayer, the prayer; fear Allah regarding those whom your right hands possess [Abu Dawud 5156; Sahih per al-Albani]. On screen: "those in your care". (scholar question Q40)

**Likely questions**
- *"What does 'those in your care' literally mean?"* Answer honestly: the Arabic literally means "those whom your right hands possess", i.e. slaves and servants. Slavery existed everywhere then; his last words urged kindness to the most vulnerable people in a household. Today the same care applies to anyone who depends on us (employees, children, the elderly). Don't claim slavery is acceptable today; detailed questions go to the imam. (scholar question Q40)
- *"What illness did he have?"* The hadith say he was in great pain at the end (he said death has its agonies [Bukhari 4449]) and that he still felt the Khaybar poison [Bukhari 4428]. Keep it brief and gentle.
- *"Did he want to write something at the end?"* There is a well-known report about this; it's a matter of long-standing disagreement between Muslim groups, and this track leaves it out. Suggest the imam if they want to study it.
- *"How do I keep praying when life is heavy?"* Listen first. All five are due, and it's fine to do them simply; pray wherever you are when it's time (Days 8–30). For specific situations (hospital, work, travel), the imam can advise. If they're overwhelmed, involve the mentor.
- *"I'm caring for a sick or dying non-Muslim parent."* Caring for them is part of their faith [Q 31:14–15]; comfort first. Questions about the parent's fate are never answered here (Day 77; Q23 handling via the imam).

**Escalate:** detailed questions on slavery (Q40); a convert caring for a dying relative who seems overwhelmed (mentor); any question about a relative's fate (Day 77 handling, imam).

**Don't**
- Don't tell the "pen and paper" incident (log row X22) or discuss succession.
- Don't describe his suffering in detail.
- Don't use "those whom your right hands possess" on a screen.
